cur:catacombs-arles-chair-of-peter.summary: A continuous frieze of figures shows Christ working miracles among the apostles together with scenes of Peter, from whom the sarcophagus takes its name. Dense and animated, it reflects the Roman Constantinian style that spread to Arles.
facts: The museum dates it to the 330s.
Its traditional name refers to a scene of Peter, the founder of the Roman see.
cur:catacombs-arles-chair-of-peter.notes: Scenes not verified one by one.

cur:manuscripts2-utrecht-psalm-13-christ.summary: The cross-nimbed Christ-Logos sits in a globe-mandorla among angels and looks down on a world in which 'there is none that doeth good': a tyrant enthroned under a serpent-twined canopy, soldiers holding up severed heads, and the poor oppressed. The young psalmist turns to him in supplication and points to these scenes of evil. The same composition was reused, with variations, for the almost identical Psalm 52.
facts: The Utrecht Psalter illustrates every psalm and canticle with a lively pen drawing — 166 in all — that translates the words of the text, often literally, into images; in these the Lord of the psalms is regularly shown as the youthful Christ-Logos.
It reached Canterbury by about 1000, where it was copied three times in the Middle Ages: the Harley Psalter, the Eadwine Psalter and the Anglo-Catalan Psalter.
cur:manuscripts2-utrecht-psalm-13-christ.notes: The figure of the Lord is identified as Christ (the Christ-Logos) following the commentary of the Utrecht University Library's annotated edition, which describes the psalter's consistent practice of drawing the God of the psalms as the youthful Christ. The image is a crop of the drawing from the library's IIIF image server.

cur:manuscripts2-paris-gregory-adoration.summary: In the top register the Magi, led by an angel, bring their gifts to the Virgin, who sits holding the Christ child, with Joseph standing beside her. The lower registers show Herod ordering the Massacre of the Innocents, the flight of Elizabeth with the infant John, and the martyrdom of Zacharias. Much of the paint has flaked away, but the haloed Virgin and Child remain clear.
facts: The Paris Gregory was commissioned by Patriarch Photios as a gift for Emperor Basil I between 879 and 883 and is one of the most ambitious Byzantine manuscripts to survive from the generation after Iconoclasm.
Many of its full-page miniatures do not illustrate Gregory's sermons directly but set biblical and historical scenes beside them as a commentary devised for the court.
cur:manuscripts2-paris-gregory-adoration.notes: Folio 137r according to the Commons detail file of the same page; the Commons file name gives the Gallica view number (287).
